title: Purely inseparable degree p
statement: Let $p$ be prime and let $A\to B\to C$ be injective local maps of complete discrete valuation rings [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-pbc-adically-complete-ring], with fraction fields $K\subseteq L\subseteq M$ [def-pc-field-extension], and $M/L$ finite. Write $k_R=R/\mathfrak m_R$ for a residue field. Assume $\mathfrak m_AB=\mathfrak m_B$ and $\operatorname{char}(k_A)=p$. For a finite extension $K_1/K$ put $A_1=\operatorname{IntCl}_{{K_1}}(A)$, $L_1=(L\otimes_KK_1)_{\mathrm{red}}$, $M_1=(M\otimes_KK_1)_{\mathrm{red}}$, and let $B_1,C_1$ be the integral closures of $B,C$ in these reduced algebras [def-weil-pbc-integral-closure, def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. A finite separable extension is totally ramified with respect to a complete DVR when its integral closure is a DVR with unchanged residue field and ramification index equal to the field degree; the ramification index $e$ is defined by $\mathfrak m_R S=\mathfrak m_S^e$. A field extension is normal if every irreducible polynomial over the base with a root in the extension splits there. Assume $M/L$ is purely inseparable of degree $p$ (so characteristic $p$ and $x^p\in L$ for every $x\in M$). For any uniformizer $t$ of $A$, at least one of the following holds: (i) $\mathfrak m_AC=\mathfrak m_C$; (ii) $C=B[t^{1/p}]$ as subrings of $M$; (iii) there is a degree-$p$ separable totally ramified $K_1/K$ for which $L_1,M_1$ are fields and $A_1\to B_1\to C_1$ are maps of complete DVRs with $\mathfrak m_{A_1}B_1=\mathfrak m_{B_1}$ and $\mathfrak m_{B_1}C_1=\mathfrak m_{C_1}$ [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension].

source.place: Tag 09EY, lemma-purely-inseparable-case, specialized to complete B (hence Nagata); its three alternatives, with complete integral closures.

proof.text: The nontrivial purely inseparable extension forces $L$, hence $B,A,K$, to have characteristic $p$. By complete-DVR normalization, $C$ is the integral closure of $B$ in $M$. Write $t=vz^e$ in $C$, with $z$ a uniformizer and $v$ a unit, using the DVR valuation description (every nonzero element of a DVR is a unit times a power of a uniformizer). If $e=1$, then $tC=\mathfrak m_C$ and (i) holds. Otherwise $z^p\in L$, and the restricted valuation is $v_C(x)=e v_B(x)$ for $x\in L^\times$: write $x=t^j a$ with $a\in B^\times$ and use locality. Thus $p=v_C(z^p)=e v_B(z^p)$, so primality gives $e=p$. Consequently $z^p=ut$ with $u\in B^\times$. Also $z\notin L$ since its valuation is 1, whereas every nonzero element of $L$ has valuation divisible by $p$. The $p$ powers $1,z,\ldots,z^{p-1}$ are linearly independent over $L$ because their nonzero multiples have distinct valuations modulo $p$; a sum with a unique least valuation cannot be zero. As $[M:L]=p$, they form a basis and $M=L[z]\simeq L[Z]/(Z^p-ut)$.

source.place: Tag 09EY, opening paragraph; valuation calculation of Tag 09E6, lemma-ramification-index-a-power-of-p, written explicitly for exponent one.

proof.text: Put $D=B[S]/(S^p-t)$ and write $s$ for the class of $S$. The uniformizer-root algebra lemma says $D$ is a DVR with uniformizer $s$ and is a domain. Since $t=s^p$, the map $B\to D$ is local. Its fraction field $E=L[s]$ has degree $p$: reduce coefficients to the monic basis $1,s,\ldots,s^{p-1}$, whose independence also follows from their distinct valuations modulo $p$. Complete-DVR normalization identifies $D$ with the complete integral closure of $B$ in $E$. Apply the Frobenius-digit lemma to $B\subset D$ and $u$. This either produces a finite expansion $u=\sum_{i<m}b_i^pt^i+bt^m$ with nonpower residue of $b$, treated in steps 4 onward, or gives $w\in D$ with $w^p=u$.

source.place: Tag 09EY, last two paragraphs, using Tag 09EV, lemma-pull-root-uniformizer, for the complete root algebra.

proof.text: In the root case, $(ws)^p=ut$. Hence the presentation in step 1 embeds $M$ into $E$ by $z\mapsto ws$. Both fields have degree $p$ over $L$, so this embedding is onto. Transporting $s$ back to $M$ gives its unique $p$th root of $t$. Under the same embedding, complete-DVR normalization identifies $C$ with $D$. Thus $C=B[t^{1/p}]$, which is (ii).

source.place: Tag 09EY, final paragraph, corrected complete-ring argument with the root taken in B[t^(1/p)].

proof.text: In the finite-expansion case choose $n=m+2$. The separable-approximation lemma gives $K_1/K$, a complete DVR $A_1$, and a uniformizer $s$ with $t=s^p+s^{np}a$, $a\in A_1$. This extension has degree $p$, unchanged residue field, and ramification index $p$, as required. Apply totally ramified base change to $A\to B$: $L_1=L\otimes_KK_1$ is a field and its integral closure $B_1=B\otimes_A A_1$ is a complete DVR, with uniformizer $s$, residue field $k_B$, and $\mathfrak m_{A_1}B_1=\mathfrak m_{B_1}$.

source.place: Tags 09EW (lemma-make-degree-q-extension) and 09ER (lemma-weakly-unramified-goes-up-along-totally-ramified), used in the middle paragraph of 09EY.

proof.text:
Set $h=1+s^{(n-1)p}a$, so $t=s^ph$. In $B_1$ put $Q=\sum_{i<m}b_i s^{i+1}$. The Frobenius identity gives $Q^p=\sum_{i<m}b_i^p s^{(i+1)p}$. Substituting the finite expansion yields
$$ut-Q^p=b s^{(m+1)p}+\sum_{i<m}b_i^p s^{(i+1)p}(h^{i+1}-1)+b s^{(m+1)p}(h^{m+1}-1).$$
For each integer $j\geq1$, $h^j-1$ is divisible by $s^{(n-1)p}$, since $h-1$ is. Each term of the sum is therefore divisible by $s^{(i+n)p}$, hence by $s^{np}$, and the final error term is too. Thus $ut-Q^p=b s^{(m+1)p}+s^{np}d$ for some $d\in B_1$. Write $c=b+s^{(n-m-1)p}d$; then $ut-Q^p=s^{(m+1)p}c$ and $\bar c=\bar b$ in $k_{B_1}=k_B$. This is the omitted coefficient calculation, with the error exponent retained.

source.place: Tag 09EY, displayed equation followed by computation omitted; expansion carried out here. The exponent after division is (n-m-1)p.

proof.text:
Apply the nonpower-residue root lemma to $B_1$ and $c$: the algebra $L_1[Y]/(Y^p-c)$ is a field of degree $p$, and its integral closure $T$ over $B_1$ is a DVR with uniformizer $s$. The substitution $Z=Q+s^{m+1}Y$, invertible over $L_1$, gives
$$M\otimes_KK_1\simeq L_1[Z]/(Z^p-ut)\simeq L_1[Y]/(Y^p-c).$$
Thus $M_1$ is this field, without any nilpotents to remove. Complete-DVR normalization applied to $B_1\subset M_1$ identifies $T$ with its complete normalization.

source.place: Tag 09EY middle paragraph, application of Tag 09EX, lemma-pre-purely-inseparable-case, and the explicit change of generator.

proof.text: It remains to check that $T$ is the stated integral closure of $C$. For $x\in C$, step 1 makes $x$ integral over $B$, so its same monic equation has coefficients in $B_1$. Hence $C\subseteq T$. Conversely, an element integral over $C$ is integral over $T$ by its same equation, and belongs to $T$ because this DVR is integrally closed. For the other inclusion, $T$ is finite over $B_1$ by complete normalization and $B_1=B\otimes_AA_1$ is finite over $B$ by finite normalization of $A$ in $K_1$. Products of finite module generators make $T$ finite over $B$; since $B\subset C\subset T$, those same generators span it over $C$. A finite algebra is integral, so every element of $T$ is integral over $C$. Therefore $C_1=T$. Its uniformizer is $s$, the uniformizer of $B_1$, so $\mathfrak m_{B_1}C_1=\mathfrak m_{C_1}$. Together with step 4 and completeness this is (iii).

source.place: Tag 09EY, identification of the integral closure in the third alternative; complete-DVR normalizations and finite algebra integrality.
